item.title: My first lesson in going direct came off a French market stall, watching my dad sell Drago…
item.description:
My first lesson in going direct came off a French market stall, watching my dad sell Dragon Ball Z toys. I was six.
This was in Dieppe, a little French seaside town by the coast.
I used to ride along on the supply runs, sat up front in this massive van while he worked out what to buy and what would actually shift that weekend.
Then I'd sit at the stall and watch him sell.
My brother was the hands-on one (he'd actually be serving, I was more of a watcher)... but I took all of it in. The way he read people. The way he'd land on a price without it ever turning into a haggle.
I've got this memory of being on his lap steering that van, hands barely reaching the wheel.
None of it felt like anything at the time. It was just Saturdays with my dad.
I build a company now on the whole idea that you go direct, nothing sat between you and the person actually buying.
Turns out I had a front row seat to that every weekend, off a fold-out table in a French market.

item.title: It took 1.9 billion tokens to edit our first podcast episode with AI. Someone worked out i…
item.description:
It took 1.9 billion tokens to edit our first podcast episode with AI.
Someone worked out it was AI from one sound effect:
We recorded the episode this month, paid an agency to cut it, and then I sat down and cut the same footage myself with an AI to see what was left of that job.
The machine had every advantage. All seventy two minutes of footage, the full transcript, and a specification we had built by taking one of the best podcast openings in the world apart and measuring what it actually does.
Then I put both versions online without saying which was which.
The first reply:
"2 is the AI right? 1 feels more traditional and 2 feels very overdone, and that sound effect is pretty bad."
Three judgements in one sentence, and all three of them correct.
The sound effect is the one I keep coming back to.
I had been saying our transitions sounded fake for a while. I could hear it. I could not name it.
When we finally measured them, almost all of the energy was sitting up in the high frequencies with nothing underneath it.
A phone speaker cannot reproduce the top end. So what reaches the listener is a thin hiss where a thud should be.
Nearly two billion tokens, and it gave itself away on a whoosh.
It did not lose everywhere. The overlays it built are genuinely good and I would ship those exactly as they came out.
But we are running the agency's version, and the second person to reply summed that one up too. Better, he said, if a bit unoriginal.
He is right as well. It has all the retention editing and none of the care.
So we paid for one and built the other, and neither of them is good.
Most of what you scrolled past today was made the same way, by someone who could not hear what was wrong with it.
Go and play the last thing you published through a phone speaker with the volume low. You will hear something you have been missing.

item.title: "Hey Sakib, we're gonna terminate your contract." I was 22, on £87k, and I could do the jo…
item.description:
"Hey Sakib, we're gonna terminate your contract."
I was 22, on £87k, and I could do the job. They walked me out anyway, and it was the one decision I couldn't make myself:
The room had a laptop already open on the table and the head of HR sat behind it.
Proper American style. Badge, box, door.
I had Simply Smashed running the whole time.
I'd sit in sprint planning half-listening to a roadmap while working out how many patties we needed for Saturday.
Then I'd be round the back of the restaurant between orders, answering Slack threads about product specs off my phone.
Two lives at once and not really present in either.
I wasn't sleeping.
My joints were flaring up from carrying both, and some days I could barely walk to the office.
And I could feel it getting worse every week.
But you don't walk away from £87k at 22 when you're from where I'm from.
That number means the plan is working, even when it very clearly isn't.
So I stayed, and gave neither thing what it needed, until someone with a laptop made the call for me.
Getting walked out of a job you know you can do is not something you shake off quickly.
Especially when part of you already suspected you didn't belong there. I had a lot of imposter syndrome in that job, and being shown the door felt like confirmation.
But a few months later I went all in on Simply Smashed, and it became the highest rated burger joint in London. 4.9 stars, three thousand reviews.
None of that happens if I'm still half-listening in sprint planning.
I'm a good deal more confident now. Most of it came from being made to find out what I could do without a salary telling me.
Every bet since, including the company I'm building now, has been bigger than the one before it.
Someone had to fire me before I'd let myself go. I'd rather you didn't wait for that.

item.title: Years before Simply Smashed I built a little app, and one day the users started throwing p…
item.description:
Years before Simply Smashed I built a little app, and one day the users started throwing people out. I never told them to.
It was called MiniDeed. Every like was a real penny to charity, and I've told the origin story on here before, so I'll skip to the part I got wrong.
We went viral during Ramadan. 47,000 posts, 26 countries, eight hundred thousand taps.
And the part I didn't see coming was what people did with the place once they were in it.
Someone would post something a bit off. Within the rules, but not in the spirit of the thing.
And before we'd even seen it, other users would step in.
"This isn't what this is for."
Nobody asked them to. They'd bought into it hard enough to guard it themselves.
It felt incredible. It was also the ceiling.
Because we were trying to crack the algorithm and reach new kinds of people, and we'd quietly built a room that only fit one kind.
Everyone else could feel it from the door.
For ages I filed that under mistakes.
I've stopped, because I now sit on calls every week with founders trying to build something for everyone, and I recognise the trap from the other side.
A product that everyone finds acceptable has nobody guarding it.
The one that a specific group would run through a wall for gets guarded for free, and it also gets a ceiling. You do not get one without the other.
I'd take the wall-runners every time now. I just wish I'd known I was choosing.

item.title: "Don't stay too long in this place." A stranger at Goldman Sachs said that to me in my fir…
item.description:
"Don't stay too long in this place."
A stranger at Goldman Sachs said that to me in my first week, just after showing me the prayer room. I was 18 and it took me years to work out what he meant.
I'd asked where I could pray, and they'd gone and found a Muslim on the floor to walk me down.
He pointed at the door, said that one line, and left.
I had no idea what he was on about.
I was the eager one. I'd got in off Bs and Ds at A-level and I wanted everything that building had to teach me.
I still think about him.
Because a couple of years in I noticed something I couldn't explain.
I was the only one of my uni friends earning properly, and I was saving less than all of them.
I had the job everyone wanted and somehow less time than anyone.
Nothing was wrong on paper. It just didn't add up.
There's a word for what was missing, and it's barakah.
Blessing, roughly. The thing that makes a small amount go a long way, and whose absence makes a large amount quietly disappear.
Goldman gave me more than I could have asked for at that age.
What he was pointing at was subtler. Some environments cost you more than they pay, and you only see the bill years later.
I never took it as a reason to leave.
I took it as a reason to become so good at the job that nobody could question the half hour I took to pray.
If you're the top performer on the team, even the manager who'd rather you didn't goes quiet about it.
Become undeniable first, and then you get to be fully yourself.
P.S. the same prayer room is where I met the man I'd build my first startup with. Some environments take from you. Some rooms inside them give it all back.

item.title: I was running the highest rated burger joint in London when I took a part-time job at some…
item.description:
I was running the highest rated burger joint in London when I took a part-time job at someone else's agency.
It was a junior role. I wanted it anyway, and it took me until Saturday to explain properly why.
Simply Smashed had grown on storytelling.
No marketing budget, just me telling people what we were building and letting them watch.
It worked, and honestly I had no idea why it worked.
I was doing the whole thing on instinct.
Then my brother introduced me to someone doing the same job for a living, for founders backed by YC and a16z.
That someone was Mustafa.
So I asked for a job. (part time, obviously, I still had a kitchen to run)
I could have let the title get in the way... owner of a restaurant, going back to do someone else's writing on the side. Plenty of people would have, and fair enough.
But I'd been guessing since day one, and here was a room full of people who'd stopped guessing.
The things I learned in that building do not exist on Google and they are not in ChatGPT.
How a founder actually decides what to say. What a good week of posts looks like from the inside. Which stories are ready and which ones need another month living in someone's head.
None of that is written down anywhere, because the people who know it are too busy doing it.
Before long they had me training the other writers, which still makes me laugh a bit given how I got in the door.
Then Mustafa and I left to build our own thing.
I think about this a lot now that the tools make everyone feel like an expert by lunchtime. (me included, some days)
The model will get you sixty percent of the way.
The other forty is in a room somewhere, with people who've done it, and the only way in is to go and be junior for a bit.
Most people won't tbh. Their title's in the way.
P.S. I was taking some of those a16z calls from a corner of the restaurant with noise-cancelling headphones on. That story's on here somewhere if you scroll back far enough.
